summary: This note covers the history and rationale of raising the school leaving age in England and Wales. It explains that the age has been raised many times since the 19th century, most recently in 2015, usually to build skilled labour and reduce unemployment among 16 to 18 year-olds. It also describes the Education Act 1944, which set the leaving age at 15 and was delayed by World War II, and recommended part-time education to 18 that was later dropped to cut spending.
one_line: Overview of how and why England and Wales raised the school leaving age over the 19th and 20th centuries, including the 1944 Education Act.
key_facts: The school leaving age in England and Wales has been raised numerous times over the 19th and 20th centuries, with the last raising in 2015.
Past age raisings were mainly justified by the need to generate more skilled labour by giving students more time to gain skills and qualifications.
Most 16 to 18 year-olds were not motivated to continue education after completing their GCSEs, which was seen as increasing the overall unemployment rate.
The British government hoped that making education compulsory up to age 17 by 2013 and age 18 by 2015 would change this.
In 1944, Rab Butler introduced the Education Act 1944.
The Education Act 1944 included the introduction of the Tripartite System and raised the school leaving age to 15.
The Education Act 1944 was supposed to take effect from September 1939 but was not implemented because of the effects of World War II.
The Education Act 1944 was eventually enforced from April 1947.
The comprehensive school system has since replaced the Tripartite System across most of England.
The Education Act 1944 recommended compulsory part-time education for all children until age 18.
The part-time education recommendation was dropped, similarly to the 1918 Act, to cut spending after World War II.
